summaries.example: Imagine two children applying for the same school club. One rule says anyone may apply, and another says members are chosen for skills that help with the club’s work. A different view asks whether both children had a fair chance to learn those skills. They may agree that the chance should be fair but disagree about what fairness requires.
summaries.summary: Equality of opportunity is about deciding which differences should and should not affect people’s chances to get valuable goods or positions. For example, many people think a job should not be closed to someone because of an unfair rule or discrimination. Some think it is enough that the job is legally open to everyone. Others say people also need a realistic chance to gain the needed skills, and that social class, education, family life, or other conditions can make chances unequal. Another view says applicants should be chosen by relevant ability and effort. The most demanding view discussed says that differences should result only from people’s responsible choices, not from luck. These ideas do not all agree, so “equality of opportunity” is a family of related ideas rather than one simple rule.
key_ideas: People often support equality of opportunity while disagreeing about what counts as a fair opportunity.
Some views focus on fair rules for choosing people; others focus on whether society gives people fair chances overall.
Views range from thin rules, such as removing official barriers, to thicker views that also consider education, family background, class, and other influences.
Equality of opportunity may concern competitive goods, such as jobs, or non-competitive goods, such as eligibility for support.
Family life can give children different advantages, so equality of opportunity may conflict with family freedom and care.
A very demanding view says that only people’s responsible choices should affect how well they fare, though applying this idea is difficult.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rules about opportunity affect schools, jobs, elections, healthcare, and many other parts of life. They help us ask whether a difference in success comes from a fair reason or from an unfair obstacle. Thinking carefully also shows that making opportunities fair may require more than removing a rule that says “you cannot enter.” It may raise hard questions about family help, social class, discrimination, and how much society should change to give people fair chances.

important_terms.definition: The idea that some differences in people’s success may be acceptable if people had a fair chance to pursue the same good or position.
A result in which people receive the same amount or status. Equality of opportunity does not always require this.
A chance to get a good or position. It is more than a bare possibility, but it does not promise success.
A view saying that a position should be open to everyone and that the best-qualified person should be chosen.
A view saying that people should have a genuinely fair chance to develop and use their abilities, not merely be allowed to enter a contest.

questions_to_think_about: Is it enough that everyone is allowed to enter a competition, or must everyone also have similar chances to prepare?
Should a school choose the student with the highest score, or should it consider unequal chances to learn?
Can families give special help to their own children while society still aims for fair opportunity?
Which differences in success should count as fair?

summaries.example: Suppose a university uses school grades to select students for a mathematics program. A formal view may ask whether the program is open to all and whether applicants are judged without direct discrimination. A meritocratic view adds that the strongest candidates for the course should be selected. A substantive view asks whether unequal schooling made the grades an unreliable sign of ability. The university might respond by using a better test, or it might use group preferences to offset unequal educational chances. Each response protects a different aspect of equality of opportunity.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry explains that equality of opportunity is a contested family of ideas, unified by the thought that some inequalities in prospects are justified while others arise from inappropriate determinants. One distinction is between deontic views, which regulate selection and distribution procedures, and telic views, which evaluate the structure of people’s opportunities overall. Formal equality may prohibit legal exclusion, coercion, nepotism, and some forms of discrimination. Meritocratic equality adds selection by qualifications relevant to a role, but it leaves open how society creates roles, defines qualifications, and rewards them. Substantive views hold that access must be meaningful: people need a realistic ability to develop the qualifications used in competition. Rawls’s fair equality of opportunity requires that social class not reduce the prospects of people with similar talent and willingness to use it. Radical or luck-egalitarian views go further, treating natural and social circumstances as unfair sources of unequal prospects and allowing choice to determine differences. The entry also examines family life, affirmative action, and whether the ideal applies to particular goods, all goods, or people across national borders.
key_ideas: The central dispute is not usually whether opportunity matters, but which factors are illegitimate obstacles to success.
Formal equality can remove legal barriers and direct discrimination while leaving major differences in preparation and realistic prospects.
Meritocratic equality adds selection by qualifications relevant to the role, but it does not by itself determine which roles exist or how they should be rewarded.
Substantive views ask whether people can actually develop the abilities needed to compete; Rawls’s fair equality of opportunity gives special attention to social class.
Deontic fairness in procedures and telic fairness in overall prospects can come apart, creating disagreement about hiring, admissions, and corrective policies.
Luck egalitarian views distinguish brute luck from option luck, but choices are often made under unequal circumstances, making responsibility difficult to assess.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept guides arguments about education, employment, political office, healthcare, family policy, and corrective measures such as affirmative action. Distinguishing its versions prevents a shallow agreement from hiding serious disagreement. For example, removing formal barriers may still leave class-based differences in skill development; selecting the best-qualified applicant may improve procedure while failing to equalize prospects; and group preferences may improve fair chances while departing from a strict merit criterion. The concept therefore helps connect questions about discrimination and selection with wider questions about social structure, responsibility, freedom, and justice

important_terms.definition: A broad ideal under which some inequalities in success are permitted, but certain factors are judged illegitimate influences on people’s prospects.
A conception focused on rules and decisions for allocating positions or goods, including which selection criteria are permissible.
A conception focused on whether people enjoy equal opportunities as a condition of society overall.
A family of views holding that opportunities are equal when positions are open to all, though background conditions may still make success very unequal.
The view that open competitions should select people according to qualifications relevant to the position.
A view requiring meaningful or realistic means to compete, including attention to background conditions that shape skills and qualifications.
Rawls’s view combining open positions with a fair chance: people with similar ability and willingness to use it should have similar prospects regardless of social class.
A view, also called luck egalitarianism, according to which unequal prospects should result only from people’s responsible choices, not from circumstances beyond their control.

questions_to_think_about: Can a competition be meritocratic if the qualifications were produced by strongly unequal schools or families?
When should a decision-maker improve a selection test, and when should it depart from merit-based selection?
Does a fair chance require equal prospects for people with similar abilities, or equal prospects more generally?
How should the value of family relationships be balanced against the unequal advantages families create?
Should equality of opportunity apply mainly within a society, or across national borders as well?

summaries.example: A school is choosing students for a robotics team. One rule says every student may try out and bans unfair treatment based on identity. Another rule says the strongest applicants should be chosen. A third rule asks whether some students had access to better equipment, coaching, or classes before the tryout. Students might agree that the team should be fair but disagree about which of these rules fairness demands.
summaries.summary: Equality of opportunity sounds simple, but philosophers use it in several ways. At its core is a question: which factors should affect a person’s chance to get a job, place, benefit, or other good, and which factors should not? A thin, formal view may require that no law or official rule blocks people from applying. A broader view may also reject nepotism and discrimination. Meritocratic equality says that, once the competition is open, people should be chosen by qualifications that matter for the position. Critics respond that people may not have had equal chances to develop those qualifications. Substantive views therefore examine education, nutrition, class, family background, and other conditions that shape realistic prospects. Rawls’s fair equality of opportunity says that people with similar abilities and willingness to use them should have similar prospects regardless of social class. Luck egalitarian views go further, arguing that differences should come only from responsible choices, not unchosen circumstances. The entry also asks whether families, affirmative action, healthcare, and opportunities across national borders belong within the idea.
key_ideas: Equality of opportunity allows some unequal results, but only when the reasons for those results are considered legitimate.
Different theories draw the line in different places: official barriers, discrimination, qualifications, social background, or luck.
Formal equality can make a contest open while leaving people with very different preparation and chances of success.
Meritocracy asks for selection by relevant qualifications, but people disagree about what counts as relevant and how qualifications should be measured.
Fair equality of opportunity looks at background conditions, especially social class and education, that shape people’s abilities and prospects.
Family choices can help children in unequal ways, creating a conflict between equal opportunity and valuable family relationships.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate affects how we judge school admissions, hiring, public benefits, and policies designed to address disadvantage. It shows why a rule can look neutral yet still produce unequal chances. It also explains why people may support “fair opportunity” but disagree about solutions: some favor better testing or education, while others support preferences for disadvantaged groups. Finally, it makes us examine a real tension between equality and freedom. Families and associations may reasonably care more about their own members, but that partiality can give some people advantages that others do not receive.

important_terms.definition: The idea that people should have fair chances to gain a position or good, even though they may not all end with the same result.
A situation where everyone receives the same amount, rank, or result. This is different from giving everyone a fair chance.
A view that focuses on whether the rules for selecting or distributing something are allowed or unfair.
A view that focuses on whether people actually have fair prospects in society, not only whether the rules look neutral.
The idea that a competition is open and that people are selected for abilities and qualifications that fit the position.
The view that formal permission to compete is not enough; people must have meaningful chances to gain the qualifications needed.
Rawls’s idea that people with similar abilities and willingness to work should have similar chances, even if they come from different social classes.
The view that luck outside a person’s control should not decide their prospects, while responsible choices may create differences.

questions_to_think_about: If everyone may join a contest, is the contest fair even when some people had much better training?
What makes a qualification relevant to a job or team?
Should schools correct for unequal home resources, or would that interfere too much with families?
Are differences caused by natural ability fair, unfair, or something in between?
Should fair opportunity mean fair chances within one country, or for people everywhere?
